title: Reading the symptoms: which memory bug is this?
objective: By the end of this lesson you can look at a crash, a wrong value, or a slowly growing process and name the likely memory defect behind it — which is the step that turns hours of guessing into a targeted search.

blocks.text: You have met each of these individually. This lesson is about telling them apart from the outside, because in real work you rarely start with the bug — you start with a symptom, and the diagnosis decides where you look.

rows: Crash at a line that looks fine
Corruption caused earlier and elsewhere
The last write to a nearby buffer
A value changes with nothing writing to it
Overflow from an adjacent buffer
The neighbouring variable in the same struct or frame
Works alone, breaks when called twice
Use after free, or a stale pointer into a reused block
What was freed between the two calls
Memory grows steadily under load
Leak on a path taken repeatedly
The error path that returns without freeing
Works at -O0, breaks at -O2
Undefined behaviour the optimiser assumed away
Signed overflow, aliasing, uninitialised reads
Different result on each run
Uninitialised memory being read
A declaration with no initialiser
Crash inside malloc or free itself
The allocator's bookkeeping was corrupted earlier
A heap overflow or a double free before this point

blocks.title: The crash location is usually not the bug location
blocks.text: Memory corruption separates cause from effect. A write that goes four bytes too far may do nothing for a million instructions and then take down an unrelated function. This is the single most important thing to internalise: when a crash makes no sense at the line it happened on, stop reading that line and start looking for who wrote nearby.
The five patterns, in one place

blocks.caption: 1 — Out-of-bounds write
lines: int  is_admin = 0;             /* often sits right next to it in the frame */
/* is_admin may now be non-zero, and nothing wrote to it directly. */

blocks.caption: 2 — Use after free
lines: /* ...some other code allocates and gets the same block... */
s->user_id = 1;                /* writing into whatever now lives there */

blocks.caption: 3 — Double free
lines: free(buffer);              /* second free — corrupts allocator metadata */

blocks.caption: 4 — Leak on the error path
lines: return -1;                 /* buf leaks — every failed parse loses 1KB */

blocks.caption: 5 — Uninitialised read
lines: printf("%d\n", count);         /* if condition was false, this reads leftovers */

blocks.text: Why the same input sometimes works and sometimes does not

All five depend on what happened to be in memory at that moment. That is why these bugs are famous for appearing only in production, only under load, or only after an unrelated change: the layout shifted, and a write that was landing in unused padding is now landing on something that matters.

blocks.title: This is exactly why the sanitizers exist
blocks.text: Rather than waiting for corruption to become visible, AddressSanitizer places guard regions around every allocation and checks each access. The bug is reported at the moment it occurs, with the line that did it and the line that allocated or freed the memory. The next lesson is entirely about using these tools well.

items: Reproduce it reliably — an intermittent bug you cannot trigger is a bug you cannot verify you fixed
Rebuild with -fsanitize=address,undefined and run again; most of the time you are finished here
If it only appears at -O2, suspect undefined behaviour and run the undefined-behaviour sanitizer specifically
If memory grows over time, run under a leak checker with a realistic workload, not a single request
Only then start reading code — and read the writes near the corrupted data, not the line that crashed

blocks.title: Cause each symptom, then diagnose it blind
steps: Compile the is_admin example with AddressSanitizer and confirm an out-of-bounds report; do not rely on a particular neighbouring variable changing
Write the use-after-free example, run it plainly, then under -fsanitize=address
Write a leak inside a loop and watch memory grow with: ./prog & then top or ps
Write the uninitialised read and run it several times — note the value changing
Write a signed overflow check and compare -O0 with -O2 output
For each one, write down the symptom first, then confirm the sanitizer names the cause you expected
blocks.expected: Five failures you produced on purpose, each with a symptom you can now recognise from the outside. The value here is the mapping: symptom to suspect, before you have read a single line of the code that broke.

cheatsheet: The crash location is usually not the bug location
A value changing with no write to it = an overflow from a neighbour
Breaks only on the second call = use-after-free or a stale pointer
Steady growth under load = a leak on a frequently taken path, usually an error path
Works at -O0, breaks at -O2 = undefined behaviour the optimiser assumed away
Different result each run = an uninitialised read
Crash inside malloc/free = the heap metadata was corrupted earlier
Reproduce, then rebuild with sanitizers, then read code — in that order

checkpoint.prompt: A program crashes on a line that is clearly correct. What does that suggest?

choices.A: The line needs a NULL check
choices.B: Memory was corrupted earlier somewhere else, and this line is merely where the damage became visible

checkpoint.explanation: Corruption separates cause from effect. Look for the write that went out of bounds, not at the line that finally tripped over the result.

checkpoint.prompt: A service works fine in testing and slowly consumes memory in production. Which defect fits?

choices.C: A leak on a path taken repeatedly

checkpoint.explanation: Often an error path that returns before freeing. Steady growth under load points to an allocation that is never released on a path that runs often. Error paths are the usual suspects because they are the least tested.

checkpoint.prompt: Code works at -O0 and misbehaves at -O2. What is the first suspicion?

choices.A: Undefined behaviour that the optimiser is allowed to assume never happens, such as signed overflow or an uninitialised read

checkpoint.explanation: Optimisers rewrite code on the assumption that undefined behaviour does not occur. When that assumption is wrong, behaviour changes with the optimisation level.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the correct order when diagnosing a suspected memory bug?

choices.A: Increase the stack size and retry
choices.B: Reproduce reliably, rebuild with sanitizers, then read the code around what they report
choices.C: Read the code carefully, then add printf statements, then guess

checkpoint.explanation: The tools give you the exact line and the exact allocation. Reading code first means searching a large space for something the sanitizer would have pointed at in seconds.
